canonicalExplanation.summary: CSS lengths have different **reference points**. `px` is a fixed CSS pixel. `rem` is relative to the **root** font size (usually 16px, and it grows when users raise their browser's text size). `em` is relative to the **current element's** font size (for font-size itself, the parent's). `%` is relative to the parent (for width). `vw`/`vh` are 1% of the viewport. Choose each unit for what the value should **follow**.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner with low vision sets their browser's default text to 24px. On your site, nothing changes — every font size is in px. Meanwhile, your padding in `em` grows oddly inside large headings. Units decide who follows whom. Body text uses rem for user-scalable sizing, while a border uses px for a stable, one-device-pixel-like design choice. In this lesson you'll select and justify units for readable text, spacing and responsive dimensions.

```predict
{"question": "Root font is 16px; a heading has `font-size: 2rem` and `padding: 1em`. Padding in px?", "options": ["16px", "32px"], "answer": 1, "why": "The heading's font-size is 2rem = 32px, and em for padding is relative to the element's own font size: 1em = 32px."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Rules, declarations and values** and **Content, padding, border and margin** — units size those layers.

sections.heading: The model: each unit has a reference
sections.body:
| Unit | Relative to | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| `px`. | fixed CSS pixel. | hairline borders, small fixed details. |
| `rem`. | root font size. | body text, spacing scales — respects user settings. |
| `em`. | the element's font size. | padding that should scale with that element's text. |
| `%`. | the containing block (for width). | fluid widths. |
| `vw` / `vh`. | 1% of viewport width/height. | full-screen sections, fluid type with clamp(). |
| `ch`. | width of "0". | line length, e.g. max-width: 65ch. |

```css
body     { font-size: 1rem; }                   /* follows user setting */
.btn     { padding: 0.5em 1em; }                 /* scales with button text */
.divider { border-top: 1px solid #d1d5db; }      /* stays thin */
h1       { font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 4vw, 3rem); } /* fluid but bounded */
```

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why not use vw alone for font size?", "answer": "Pure vw text doesn't respond to browser zoom preferences and can become tiny on phones or huge on wide screens. Combine with rem inside clamp()."}
```

sections.heading: rem vs em in nesting

includes: Choose px, rem, em, %, vw/vh and ch based on what a value should follow.
Respect user font-size preferences and avoid em compounding.
excludes: Physical units like cm and in.

outcomes: Select and justify units for readable text, spacing and responsive dimensions.

examples.title: rem for text, px for a hairline border
examples.situation: Body text uses rem for user-scalable sizing while a border uses px for a stable one-device-pixel-like design choice.
walkthrough: **Body text uses rem:** `body { font-size: 1rem }` — at a 24px browser default it becomes 24px, so user-scalable sizing works.
**Border uses px:** `.divider { border-top: 1px solid }` stays thin at any text size — a stable design choice.
**Test:** set the browser's default font to 24px; the browser will render larger text while dividers stay hairline.
examples.result: Text respects the learner's settings, and decorative borders stay crisp.

examples.title: The fixed-pixel form
examples.situation: A form sets every label, input and button to `font-size: 14px`. Users who increased default text see no change.
walkthrough: px ignores the browser's default font-size preference.
Page zoom still works, but text-size settings don't.
Fix: convert to rem (14px ≈ 0.875rem) and re-test with a 20px default.
examples.result: The form's text now grows with the user's chosen size.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: rem and em always resolve to the same font-size reference.
misconceptions.correction: rem is always relative to the root element's font size; em is relative to the current element's font size (or the parent's for font-size itself), so em values compound in nested elements.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why was 1em equal to 32px?

analogy.example: Units are like **measuring in different ways**: px is a fixed ruler, rem is "a portion of the house's standard size", em is "a portion of this room's size", vw is "a portion of the window". Pick the one whose reference should change the value.
limitations: Rulers don't care about user preferences; rem does.
Rooms inside rooms is exactly how em compounds.

steps.explanation: The learner raises the browser's default text size.
Body text uses rem for user-scalable sizing, so it follows the setting.
The border uses px for a stable, one-device-pixel-like design choice.

remediation.explanation: For each length ask: **Should this grow with the user's text size (rem), with this element's text (em), with its container (%), with the screen (vw), or stay fixed (px)?**

recap.summary: To select and justify units, use rem for readable text and spacing that respects user settings, em for values that scale with an element's own text, % and vw for fluid dimensions (bounded with clamp), ch for line length, and px for small fixed details like borders.
